              The bank generally puts in all or most of the equity in the CDO. The mez-
              zanine and senior notes are sold to investors. Insurance companies, fund
              managers and high net worth individuals buy these notes. For some
              obscure reason retirees and wealthy individuals in Australia and New
              Zealand are especially attracted to CDO mezzanine investments.
                 The senior note holders get paid first. If there are losses then equity
              takes the first losses. If the losses are greater than the equity amount then
              the mezzanine investors get hit. Senior note holders take a smack only if the
DAS_C10.QXD    5/3/07    7:59 PM      Page 287




                        9  C re d i t w h e re c re d i t i s d u e – f u n w i t h C D S a n d C D O   287




              losses on the underlying loans are above the equity and mezzanine
              amounts. The mezzanine and equity investors receive a high return in
              return for accepting the higher risk. This is tranching.
                  CDO tranching is the black art of dissimulation. Investors are told that
              they are getting access to a ‘diversified’ portfolio of credit risk and are
              promised highly customized credit risk. It’s all very clever ‘spin’.
                  The portfolio on which the CDO is based is generally ‘diversified’. For
              example, a $1,000 million portfolio might be made up of 100 loans of $10
              million each. Each loan is to a different entity; the portfolio is diversified; if
              you buy the senior notes then you are also diversified.
                  Unfortunately, if you buy the mezzanine or equity then you have a prob-
              lem. You have taken a risk on a small subset of the portfolio. Assume that if
              any of the 100 firms defaults, you would expect to lose 100% (a recovery
              rate of 0%). This means that equity investors take the risk of the first two
              firms to default ($20 million of losses). The mezzanine investor takes the
              risk of the next three firms to default ($30 million of losses).
                  Between them, equity and mezzanine investors take the risk of the first
              five firms out of the 100 firms in the portfolio to default. The problem is
              that they have no idea who these five firms are likely to be. This is the exact
              opposite of ‘diversification’, it is ‘concentration’ risk. A British regulator
              once referred to CDO equity and mezzanine as ‘toxic waste’. Credit risk is
              best taken in small, well-diluted doses.



                                                     It’s super
              Tranching also allows the manufacture of different types of credit risk. The
              senior notes are usually rated ‘AAA’ – the highest credit quality. The high
              rating is the result of using equity and mezzanine to absorb some level of
              losses, which reduces the risk of the senior note holders.
                  The mezzanine is malleable; its rating is generally anywhere between ‘A’
              and ‘B’, depending on the ‘thickness’ of the equity tranche. A thick equity
              tranche lowers the mezzanine risk, a thin one increases it. Unfortunately,
              risk and return are related. Yield-hungry investors often push the envelope.
              To get higher return, the CDO is structured with a thinner equity tranche
              to increase the risk.
                  Mezzanine investors compensate by picking highly-rated firms for the
              underlying portfolio. Perversely, the higher the credit quality of the firms,
DAS_C10.QXD    5/3/07       7:59 PM       Page 288

              the ‘thinner’ the equity piece. In the example above, the mezzanine notes
              may be rated ‘A’, the return is insufficient; to get its required return, the
              investor has to take more risk. The equity piece is thinned to an anorexic
              1% ($10 million) – the mezzanine investor gets higher return. It is also now
              exposed to losses if more than one firm out of 100 defaults. This is credit at
              the roulette table.
                  Synthetic securitization introduced even more advanced forms of
              tranche warfare. The risk allocation looked different as shown in Figure 9.5.
              Senior investors in a normal CLO weren’t taking much risk; the underlying
              portfolio was usually good quality. Equity and mezzanine took the first
              losses. The compound conservatism of the rating agencies ensured that the
              chance of losses exceeding equity and mezzanine was very, very low. It was
              easy money. Dealers figured this out quickly.

                 In a synthetic securitization, the senior tranche was much smaller. The
              sponsor bank kept the upper end of the risk, the last loss piece – this was
              the ‘super senior’ game. Given that the senior notes were rated ‘AAA‘, the
              super senior tranche was better than sex, it was as close to risk free as you
              could get. The sponsor bank didn’t have to pay investors to take risk that
              wasn’t there. It made the structure much, much cheaper.
                 Some banks had to transfer the super senior risk because regulators
              wouldn’t allow them to keep it without penalty: it was transferred to rein-

              surance companies, which got about 0.10%. The actuaries at the reinsurers
              couldn’t believe their luck. They estimated the risk at a fraction of 1 basis
              point (0.01% pa). It was a free lunch.
                 The super senior tranche subtly changed the risk for the senior note
              holders. In a synthetic securitization, the senior tranche bears the first loss
              within the senior pieces, but it’s riskier. Investors seemed unconcerned or
              oblivious to the differences in risk. Dealers won out in tranche warfare.



                                                A capital idea
              Initially, banks used CDOs to transfer the risk of loans to investors. I saw a
              few of the CDO proposals that dealers pitched to banks, trying to convince
              them to sell off their loans. The pitch was supposedly about ‘credit risk
              reduction’ but it was actually about ‘capital management’.
                  The transaction didn’t reduce the selling bank’s credit risk, it usually had
              to keep the equity piece. The first losses were for its account – this is ‘hurt
              money’ or the ‘skin in the game’. Investors want to make sure that you
              aren’t selling them a whole lot of dud loans, they want you to take the first
              loss. Generally, the first loss piece was set at a level that was way above the
              anticipated level of loan losses on the portfolio. In effect, the bank was
              keeping most of the risk.
                  A bank would generally have to hold a minimum of 8% against a loan to
              a corporation. On $1,000 billion this was $80 million. After it did the
              CDO, it would only need capital against the equity piece it was holding; if
              the equity piece was 2%, under the regulations the bank had to hold 2% or
              $20 million on $1,000 million. In the jargon, the bank had released capital
              (around $60 million).
                  The capital released was worth around $12 million a year. This assumes
              that the bank wanted to make around 20% return on capital. The CDO
              cost was about 0.35% pa on the total size of the deal – $3.5 million. The
              bank was $8.5 million ahead. Was this real money? What was the bank
              going to do with capital it freed up? The assumption was that the market
              was brimful of wonderful opportunities where the bank could invest its cap-
              ital and make more than 20% – if all else failed then it could buy back its
              own shares. The CDO freed up capital and boosted return on capital; the
              capital benefits gave CDOs ‘traction’.
DAS_C10.QXD    5/3/07   7:59 PM    Page 290




              290                        Tr a d e r s , G u n s & M o n e y




                   The synthetic securitization achieved the same things. It was much
              cheaper, the cost was around 0.10–0.15% pa or $1–$1.5 million. It offered
              all the advantages at lower cost.
                   CDOs only worked where the bank sold off the credit risk on better
              quality companies, usually investment grade (rated ‘BBB’ or better). In
              practice, these companies are less likely to default anyway. The bank was sell-
              ing off its better risks and keeping its weaker clients; it also ended up with
              the equity in the CDO. Was the bank actually better off? In the RAROC
              age, it was heresy to ask these questions. CDOs were just a capital idea.



                                       The arbitrage age
              The party almost never got started – the banks stopped selling credit risk
              almost as soon as they started. They didn’t actually have a lot of the better
              quality risks needed to make CDOs work; these clients had long ago
              bypassed the banks and raised money from investors directly. The banks had
              been ‘dis-intermediated’.
                 The capital freed up proved difficult to redeploy. Opportunities didn’t
              seem to be abundant. Repurchasing shares was okay but it was starting to
              reach absurd levels.
                 CDOs also reduced reported earnings. Equity analysts wanted banks to
              improve RAROC and keep earnings growing at an unrealistic rate. Bank
              CEOs who followed RAROC too literally were in danger of ‘shrinking
              themselves to greatness’. RAROC nirvana was $1 of income earned with
              zero capital. It was infinite RAROC. It also was fatal for the CEO.
                 The CDO age was in danger of being stillborn. Ever creative, dealers
              moved into the ‘arbitrage CDO’ period. The original CDOs had been ‘bal-
              ance sheet’ trades, banks had used them to transfer credit risk and manage
              capital. Now, dealers sniffed out ‘undervalued’ credit assets; they purchased
              the bonds using a SPV that repackaged them. The whole objective was for
              the dealer to lock in the margin between the interest from the assets and
              the interest cost of the CDO notes issued to finance the purchase. That
              margin was for the dealers. They were the arbitrageurs. The investors were
              the ‘arbitraged’.
                 The late 1990s saw unprecedented growth in arbitrage CDOs. It all
              ended as it usually does, in disaster.

                                                   Hangovers
              After a period of strong returns, the CDO market hit an iceberg around
              2000/2001. The losses were huge – one investor lost a cool $1,000 million
              plus. The reasons were clear.
                  It was the credit cycle, stupid! You were investing in credit, what did you
              expect? Defaults increased sharply as the US slipped into recession and cre-
              ative accounting compounded the losses. CDOs are also massively leveraged:
              if you buy the 2% equity in a CDO, then you are 50 times leveraged, com-
              pared to the 10 to 12 times that a normal bank uses. Losses and leverage are
              not good bedfellows. Sound, highly-rated companies also found reefs.
              Asbestos liability and the Californian electricity deregulation claimed victims.
                  As the credit cycle turned, the arbitrage CDOs were hard hit. They had
              been based on US high yield (junk) bonds. The US recession and the
              unwinding of the technology bubble saw record numbers of default.
              Contagious crises in Asia, Eastern Europe and Latin America didn’t help.
                  The credit models failed miserably. The concept of average credit losses
              proved average – it seemed the worst case was much worse. If the average
              was made of one year of very large losses and several years of no losses, then
              that didn’t work well either.
                  Some CDOs were actively managed. Managers had been appointed to
              trade the portfolios, the idea being that they would minimize losses by sell-
              ing deteriorating credits. They usually compounded losses by making
              wrong trading decisions.
                  There were ‘moral hazards’. Managers had to invest equity in the CDO
              they managed which was designed to ‘align interests’ and ‘overcome
              agency conflicts’. It was a noble idea – when credit losses wiped out equity,
              the managers lost money. It was their personal wealth, which didn’t worry
              anybody, but the incentives shifted worryingly. The managers now ramped
              up the risk; they bought a lot of lottery tickets; dodgy companies whose
              bonds were trading at 35% of face value suddenly represented compelling
              investments. If the company survived then the large gain would go to the
              equity investors, if not, then the managers were no worse off. They had
              already lost their investment. The mezzanine and senior investors would
              bear the loss.
                  Holders of senior notes didn’t actually lose money. Rising defaults
              meant that the equity and mezzanine protection was reduced; this was what
              allowed the senior debt to be highly rated. As equity disappeared and mez-
DAS_C10.QXD    5/3/07   7:59 PM    Page 292




              292                        Tr a d e r s , G u n s & M o n e y




              zanine became thinner, the senior debt was downgraded. ‘AA’ notes were
              re-rated to ‘A’ or lower. The market value of the securities plummeted.
                  The current value of the CDO senior notes showed a large mark-to-
              market loss. In some cases, the fall in credit quality meant that the investor
              couldn’t hold the securities. Selling wasn’t easy. The glib promises of
              ‘liquid’ markets proved illusory – you couldn’t stay in, you couldn’t get
              out. CDOs quickly came to stand for ‘Crisis in Debt Obligations’.



                                                    UFOs
              The losses in the early 2000s didn’t stop the market, it branched out in a
              myriad of directions. There was ABS CDOs (CDOs of asset backed securi-
              ties like MBS). There were CFOs (Collateralized Fund Obligations based
              on hedge funds and private equity funds), which was confusing as CFOs
              also stood for Commodity Fund Obligations. There were ECOs (Equity
              Collateralized Obligation based on equity options) and CCOs (Commodity
              Collateralized Obligations). I was waiting for the UFOs (Unspecified Fund
              Obligations). It would be a tranched portfolio of unknown assets. It was
              designed as a surprise for the investor.
                  The most bizarre of these new variations was the CDO2 a CDO of exist-
              ing CDO securities, especially mezzanine notes. It was a re-securitization.
              Anything with a ‘re’ in front means that you are paying two lots of fees.
                  CDO2 offered higher returns to the investor. This return came from
              buying undervalued mezzanine notes in the market. It allowed dealers to
              rid themselves of residual positions from previous transactions or inventory.
              The modelling and analysis of CDO2 transaction is demanding, no one
              agrees on how to do it. In CDO2 transactions the same names may be pres-
              ent in the original CDOs. If the underlying CDO is actively managed then
              the underlying risk may change. You have no idea exactly who you are
              taking a risk on. CDO2 are known as ‘Russian dolls’ because you keep
              taking out the dolls one by one, then, there is nothing there. CDO2 are a
              bit like that.
                  When CDO2 first appeared, Nero and I sat through a presentation on
              the subject. It was from a salesperson who talked it up endlessly. Nero
              leaned across and asked seriously, ‘Isn’t this how you get BSE?’ BSE stands
              for bovine spongiform encephalopathy (mad cow disease). We are now on
              to CDO3 or CDO Cubed (A CDO of a CDO of a CDO). This is a re-re-
              securitization. Credit and stuttering seem constant companions.

                                          Geeks with Greeks
              The market moved rapidly on to an even newer paradigm – the age of
              credit trading. Geeks bearing Greeks helped make the transition. Having
              demonstrated complete mastery of other facets of derivatives, the quants
              applied their PhDs to credit and worked out that it could be traded just like
              interest rates or currencies.
                  You couldn’t actually measure any key input: you didn’t really know how
              likely it was that Company X would default (default probability) or when
              (time to default). You didn’t know what the size of your loss would be if
              they defaulted (loss given default). You couldn’t work out what the effect of
              a default by Company X will be on Company Y (default correlation).
                  This was the ‘data paradox’. In credit markets, you cannot empirically
              validate any proposition. If you ask what the risk of Company X defaulting
              is, then it hasn’t defaulted – you can’t look at history to determine the
              probability. The data paradox did not trouble the geeks. Their training was
              not in dialectics. They started each paper with the familiar greeting to
              fellow quants, ‘Assuming the following, we can show that …’
                  The basic idea was that by trading in CDS contracts, traders could man-
              ufacture any type of credit risk that the investor wanted. The masterpiece of
              the credit trading age is the STCDO (single tranche CDO).
                  In a normal CDO, the SPV buys the loans or acquires the credit risk by
              selling protection in CDS. The SPV then sells off the risk by issuing securi-
              ties into the market; the senior and mezzanine notes are sold to investors.
              In balance sheet deals, the bank selling off its risk takes the equity; in arbi-
              trage deals, the dealer takes part or all of the equity. It’s not real money, it’s
              part of the fees it made in the deal. The essence of the normal CDO is that
              the dealer takes minimal risk. It ‘facilitates’ the transfer of credit risk to the
              investor for a gratuity.
                  A STCDO is fundamentally different. Putting together a complete
              CDO became increasingly difficult. CDOs take time to market and execute;
              it’s hard to reconcile different investors’ demands. The STCDO was ‘per-
              sonalized’ service; it was built around a single investor. The investor selected
              the underlying firms, maturity, currency, leverage and rating; the dealer
              then put together the deal. Traders used CDS in the market to hedge their
              risk. This was credit ‘on tap’, CDO ‘on demand’.
                  The trick was in the hedging. In a normal synthetic CDO, the dealer
              sold protection on all the underlying firms but in a STCDO, the dealer only
DAS_C10.QXD    5/3/07   7:59 PM    Page 294




              294                        Tr a d e r s , G u n s & M o n e y




              sold protection on some of the original names in the portfolio. Why? Let’s
              say that the STCDO is for an investor who buy $50 million of ‘AAA’ senior
              notes based on a portfolio of 100 companies for $10 million each. To get
              the rating of the investment up to ‘AAA’, you may need mezzanine and
              equity of 6% or $60 million. Assuming that if anyone defaults the loss is
              60% ($6 million), the mezzanine and equity investors will eat the first ten
              losses. The senior investor is taking the risk on the next eight or nine firms
              to default; default numbers 11 to 19. This means the dealer has to enter
              into CDS only on these firms.
                  The dealer must uses credit models to calculate the likelihood of each
              underlying credit defaulting – this is the credit delta. The delta tells you the
              likelihood of each reference entity defaulting. As time goes on and things
              change, the dealer has to manage the hedge dynamically as markets change.
              A company gets into trouble or improves. The dealer makes money by trad-
              ing in the CDS. It’s the old ‘portfolio insurance’ scam.
                  The hedging is difficult; firms tend to ‘jump to default’; dealers can’t
              adjust hedges quickly enough. It’s ‘gamma’; it’s model risk. But once one
              dealer could offer CDOs ‘on demand’, others had to follow.
                  Dealers committed millions to the ‘credit trading’ age. PhDs who had
              never made a loan or traded were hired and modelled away. A number of
              standard credit indexes emerged; these were like equity indexes – the S & P
              500 or the FTSE. The index contained a fixed basket of firms. Standardized
              CDOs were traded. Quants seized upon the availability of market prices.
              There was now ‘implied correlation’; you could back out what the market
              thought the risk of X defaulting was if Y defaulted. The problem was nobody
              could yet agree on what the correlation meant or how it should be measured.

                                 Never believe your own lies
              CDO logic is perverse. It’s a bank. You buy loans and other credit risk from
              the market, then you cut it and dice it and sell it to investors. Assume you
              buy all the tranches – equity, mezzanine and senior. In effect, you just own
              the loans; you should earn exactly the market price of the loan; it should be
              impossible to make money. Certainly, it should be impossible to make the
              profits made by credit derivative desks. Then why are CDOs so profitable?
                  The balance sheet CDOs worked because the banks saved on capital.
              The savings were large, they sweetened the returns to the investors and
              dealers helping them do the capital shuffle. The regulator and shareholders
              were footing the bill.
                  The arbitrage CDOs worked because one group of investors was buying
              risk too cheaply, generally the mezzanine investors. The senior investors
              were fairly safe. The equity was risky but you had upside. If there were no
              default then the huge leverage meant you could make 20% plus returns.
              Mezzanine investors got higher interest rates but they didn’t have the
              upside of equity. If defaults were higher than expected, they lost. They
              became the de facto equity in the CDO. Mezzanine investors had grossly
              underpriced the risk. They had written the subsidy cheques.
                  In the credit trading age, it wasn’t the capital arbitrage and it wasn’t the
              mezzanine investor, so who was it? It was the dealers. They were taking
DAS_C10.QXD    5/3/07   7:59 PM   Page 296




              296                       Tr a d e r s , G u n s & M o n e y




              massive ‘model risk’ to provide investors with higher returns. It was the
              geeks and their masters who were writing the cheques; they had placed
              their faith in the credit models; they had started to believe in their lies.
              Perversely, they were showing massive profits. That’s the beauty of mark-
              to-model. If the models fail, the profit will disappear like a chimera.
                  In 2002 and 2003, benign conditions in the credit market prevailed.
              Few companies defaulted; people became foolish or brave and lent to com-
              panies at ever lower returns; the credit spread on junk bonds reached
              record lows. Credit standards declined. Bankers talked about ‘drive-by’
              bonds; these were issues usually for weak borrowers that were announced
              and sold within hours. A telecommunications company newly out of bank-
              ruptcy rushed to issue 50-year bonds. Not satisfied with 50 years, Danish
              Oil & Natural Gas (shortened frequently to the unfortunate acronym
              ‘DONG’) issued a 1,000 year bond. Traders, with their phallocentric wit,
              immediately dubbed the bond the ‘ultra-long DONG’.
                  In 2004, one bank suddenly suffered a loss of around $50 million in a
              single day on its credit delta books. Nobody really knew why: it was the
              first tremor. In 2005, GM and Ford were downgraded to junk, triggering
              panic in credit markets. Credit spreads widened as the markets reconsidered
              the pricing of risk.
                  Investors lost money in every way possible. They had loaded up on
              CDO equity: it provided high returns where defaults were low. Some
              traders had bought the equity and sold the senior tranches to finance their
              positions. Now, the different tranches began to move in different direc-
              tions. Traders lost money on the equity as default risk increased; they also
              lost on the senior tranches as spreads on these tightened as there was a gen-
              eral flight to quality. Default correlation had broken down.
                  Hedge funds had bought GM bonds and hedged by selling equity. This
              was E2C (equity to credit). It was CSA (capital structure arbitrage). In
              2003 and 2004, it had been the hot new area but now the GM bonds fell
              in value, triggering losses. Unfortunately, GM shares went up. Kirk
              Kerkorian, a vintage equity investor, emerged as a big buyer of GM shares.
              Several hedge funds took large losses – everybody had been too clever by
              half. The banks credit delta books took large losses. Everybody had been
              copula-ed.

                                                 Russian dolls
              In December 2000, Barclays Capital, the investment banking subsidiary of
              the UK bank, launched a CDO known as CORVUS. The name means
              ‘crow’ in Latin. The tranches were rated AAA through to B. Buyers
              included HSH Nordbank, a German bank.
                  CORVUS was actually a ‘dog’ and crashed rapidly. In late 2002/early
              2003, rating agencies downgraded the notes. By September 2003, the highly
              rated senior tranches had been downgraded to ‘junk’ status (below BBB).
              The mezzanine tranches, originally rated BBB, were rated CCC or lower. It
              emerged that another Barclays CDO – NERVA – had fared similarly.
                  Investors were not amused; they had bought the senior ‘AAA’ notes
              because they were of the highest credit quality. HSH met with Barclays to
              discuss ‘ze problem’. Not having received satisfaction, HSH sued Barclays
              claiming losses of $151 million. It emerged that Hamburgische
              Landesbank, now part of HSH, was also considering its position. It had a
              $420 million investment in CORVUS and NERVA. There were rumours
              that Barclays had previously settled a claim with the European Bank for
              Reconstruction and Development.
                  HSH’s claims were based on ‘misrepresentation’. Barclays had mis-sold
              the products. Other juicy titbits surfaced. The rating agency had taken the
              unusual step of posting details of the CORVUS portfolio on its website.
              The portfolio included exposure to airlines and prefab housing in America.
              Shortly after September 11, CORVUS entered into transactions with
              Barclays that appeared to increase its exposure to aircraft leases, distressed
              telcos and emerging markets. CORVUS also had exposure to other CDOs
              sold by Barclays.
                  HSH argued that CORVUS was badly structured; it alleged that it was
              badly managed. HSH accused Barclays of dumping poor-quality assets into
              the CDO. It alleged that Barclays had breached the agreed portfolio man-
              agement guidelines that governed CORVUS. There were questions about
              the potential conflict of interest at Barclays. Commentators mused about
              the lack of disclosure and transparency.
                  Barclays argued that the losses were just due to the ‘unexpected’ down-
              turn in the credit markets, and that HSH was a sophisticated investor,
              aware of the risks. Barclays’ spin doctors blustered that ‘the allegations were
              without merit’. The bank would ‘vigorously defend’ the action. Barclays
              was ‘comfortable that these investments were not mis-sold’.

                   Barclays predictably settled with HSH weeks before the case was due to

              steps of the court: the thought of the dispute being on the front page of
              every business paper in the world is sobering. Everybody remembers
              Bankers’ Trust’s court battle with P & G. Whatever the rights and wrong,
              the realpolitik is recognized.
                   Coincidentally, a dispute between Bank of America (BoA) and Banca
              Popolare di Intra (BPI) over a series of CDOs made the papers about the
              same time. Bank of America’s spokesperson stated the bank’s intention to
              defend itself ‘vigorously’. Nobody believed them: in mid-2005, the matter
              was settled. The sudden outbreak of lawsuits raised concerns: how many of
              these once fashionable ‘structured credit products’ had been mis-sold? How
              much of the profits made by the dealers from the trades would be clawed
              back in court actions? The traders didn’t care, they had made their killings.
              Mark-to-market accounting made sure of that. Many of the traders involved
              in the trades seemed to have left the industry. They were on a beach some-
              where, enjoying their bonus.
                   CDO litigation reached pandemic status. CDO sleuths emerged, poring
              through old deals showing losses, looking for a cause of action for the
              investor. Cynics pointed out that some of the CDO hunters were actually
              professionals from yesteryear who had structured and sold similar deals in the
              first place. ‘All the better to see you with!’ As the wolf in the fairytale said.
                   CDO litigation also became more convoluted. Greenwich NatWest,
              owned by Royal Bank of Scotland, sued its lawyers, Weil Gotscal &
              Manges, alleging ‘a failure to act with reasonable care and diligence in the
              structuring and documentation’ of a CDO. Weil Gotshal & Manges found
              themselves in the unusual position of having to retain legal advisors. A
              research analyst at a US firm filed a complaint alleging that his employer
              had attempted to influence his research on CDOs contrary to the law.
              CDOs were providing gainful employment for any number of lawyers.1

              Europeans were amused when Enron and Worldcom fell. Their prejudices
              about US accounting, business ethics and American investment bankers
              were confirmed. ‘It wouldn’t happen in Europe.’ Then, Parmalat happened.
              European bankers blushed: they muttered about ‘American influence’ and

              ‘American investment banks’. A central player in the Parmalat road crash

                  Parmalat had been a common firm in CDO portfolios. Diversification of

              themselves to activity in the absence of a deadline).
                  Our legal team was modest. There was Morrison and Albert: occasion-
              ally, one other nameless solicitor would appear. Then, there was counsel,

              were the accountants. Andrews, the partner, was the constant. An ever-
              changing cast of senior managers and managers accompanied him to
              meetings, never saying a word. Then, there was me – the expert witness.
                  In comparison, the entire firm of Killem & Billem seemed to be

                                  The more things change
              While we grappled with the case, the real world moved on. The ageless
              Greenspan announced his intention to retire. Greenspan’s proclivity for
              impenetrable utterances was undiminished. In congressional testimony, he
              announced that the US housing market was charged with ‘speculative fer-
              vour’, there was no ‘bubble’ in the real estate market, it was a case of ‘froth’.3
              Commentators rushed to point out that ‘froth’ was a collection of ‘bubbles’.
                  Traders grumbled that the economy Greenspan was handing over to his
              successor was not in the healthy state that the lavish tributes to the Maestro
              seemed to assume. One commentator noted that the state of the American
              economy was neatly encapsulated by Ludwig Van Mises, an Austrian econo-
              mist from the early part of the twentieth century: ‘It may be expedient for a
              man to heat the stove with his furniture; but he should not delude himself
              by believing that he has discovered a wonderful new method of heating his
              premises.’4 One journalist even dared publish a critical review of Greenspan’s
              legacy, entitled ‘The Bubble Man’. The times were changing.
                  Hedge funds were ‘in’. Traditionally they were for the very rich, now,
              they were for everybody. This was the new democracy – if it was good
              enough for the rich then it must be good enough for everybody. What did
              Groucho Marx say about not belonging to any club that would have him as
              a member?
                  Hedge funds could short, allowing them to make money when prices
              fell; they could also leverage to enhance returns in stable markets; they also
              chased absolute return. Traditional investors had become obsessed with
              performance relative to a benchmark like the broad market index. They had
              finally figured out that beating the index by 2% when it fell 10% meant that
              you still lost 8%. Hedge fund managers’ fees were also linked to perform-
              ance. They also had their own money in the fund. Investors liked all that.
                  Traditional investors joined the rush. Conservative asset managers now
              allocated part of their funds to a new ‘asset class’ – AI (alternative invest-
              ments). Funds that couldn’t short, couldn’t leverage, couldn’t use derivatives
              instead gave their money to hedge funds who could. Some asset managers
              established FoF (fund of funds): the FoF manager selected a diverse group of
              hedge funds; they did the screening and monitored the funds. There were
              capital guaranteed hedge fund investments – you couldn’t lose your principal
              although you may end up earning nothing on your investment for ten years.
                  AI gained traction. Many ordinary investors were now paying several
              layers of fees: there was the fee to their mutual fund, there was a fee to the

                                            Hot tubbing
              I worked diligently at the case, my expert report was lodged with the court.
              The other side put on their expert, Sherman, an American ex-academic who
              had worked briefly at a dealer. In the competitive world of expert work, I
              sneered that he hadn’t been in markets recently. His last publication was in
              1987. I had discovered that Sherman’s fee was double mine.
                  I received Sherman’s report: my blood pressure increased alarmingly as I
              read the document. Expert reports are generally polite affairs: one expert
              rarely attacks the other’s opinion, the disagreements are couched in terms
              of professional courtesy. ‘So and so has perhaps placed more emphasis on
              [x] than I would personally favour.’ ‘The position presented, while within
              the range of feasible interpretations, is one that in the present circumstances
              is not entirely consistent with the facts as I understand them.’
                  It is civilized and genteel, you have a drink with the other expert after
              the matter is over, you laugh about it. Most experts know that in the litiga-
              tion game you are a sideshow, you are unlikely to have a decisive effect on
              proceedings. Nobody has a clue what you are saying.
                  Sherman’s report had dispensed with the normal form – it was an out-
              right attack. I was a ‘purist’ and ‘prone to take theoretical positions’. I
              don’t mind being called ‘scum’, but a ‘purist’ or ‘theoretician’ was just out-
              rageous. This was war.
                  Some jurisdictions require an expert’s conference, which is a meeting
              between the experts. The object is to find areas of agreement and isolate

              the differences in opinion. This assumes that there is one truth and some-

              break the silence. He would never speak unless the other side spoke; the
              longest break I remember was about five minutes. The other side always
              cracked first. He would also never interrupt the other side’s statement, ever.
              His reply to any question was always ‘Yes’, ‘No’ or ‘I don’t understand your
              point’. His voice was also soft and clinical, betraying no emotion. It was the
              ‘cold war’. I asked Morrison for any last-minute pointers. ‘My boy, we have
              full confidence in you,’ was the only guidance he offered.
                  The call was short, taking less than an hour. Typical expert conferences
              drag on but I wasn’t interested in prolonging it. I had sent over a list of issues
              for discussion. The exchanges were cryptic. I followed cold war rules: on each
              issue we either agreed or agreed to disagree; whenever Sherman tried to
              engage in further discussion, I said nothing; when he finished my standard
              response was: ‘I do not understand. We should consider the next issue.’
                  Sherman found the cold war disconcerting. ‘Are you still there?’ he fre-
              quently asked. ‘I thought the line dropped out.’ ‘You really can’t disagree
              on such a fundamental point. We need to work through this point.’ ‘I don’t
              agree. We should consider the next issue.’ The cryptic responses were not
              conducive to debate. You could hear the deflation in Sherman’s voice – he
              was getting irritable. I was enjoying myself.

                  Upon reaching the end of the list, I ended the conference call abruptly.
              ‘That covers all the issues for discussion. Thank you. Goodbye.’ I then
              hung up quickly. The next day, Sherman sent an email entreating a further
              conference call. I refused, I had had enough hot tubbing for the moment.
                  A lawyer once told me that litigation is related to chaos theory, there was
              order in disorder. Success often depended upon the ability to cause unlim-
              ited chaos. Chaos was used to destabilize the opponent, the basic rule of
              guerrilla warfare.
                  The experts had to prepare a joint report for the court outlining areas of
              agreement and disagreement. I sent off my draft immediately after the con-
              ference call; I had actually prepared it earlier and it required minimal
              change. The accompanying email thanked Sherman for his participation:
              unless he had any issues we would lodge the report that day. Pressure is an
              interesting thing. Howls of protest issued forth. Sherman was not satisfied
              with the joint report.
                  The expert conference is meant to be for the experts only, lawyers are
              not allowed to attend. This is difficult to police in a conference call and I
              had had a feeling that there had been somebody in the room in London. I
              spoke to Morrison – he was delighted. He fired off a letter accusing the
              other side of ‘bad faith’. The howls of protest got louder. Morrison was
              hugely satisfied.
                  The joint report went back and forth; Sherman didn’t agree. I just sent
              the same email back each time. ‘I am entirely satisfied that the draft accords
              with my recollections and my contemporaneous notes.’ Negotiations are
              about patience – you wear out the other side. If they didn’t like my draft
              then they were free to lodge their own version. They would have to say that
              the experts couldn’t even agree on their recollection of the meeting; we
              would both look bad. The judge didn’t like us anyway. It was pure
              brinkmanship.
                  A ‘personal’ email arrived. It was conciliatory, Sherman appealed to a
              ‘higher’ interest. He could live with my draft reluctantly, provided I made some
              minor concessions; I agreed to a few changes. The email had been ‘sent from a
              BlackBerry’. In the new millennium, anybody who wanted to be somebody
              had a BlackBerry, a hand-held portable email device. Traders and business
              executives sat silently, heads bowed, squinting at the BlackBerry in their hands,
              their fingers moving tediously as – letter by letter – they tapped out an email.
              This was the BlackBerry prayer; it could happen anywhere, at meetings, confer-
              ences, buses, trains and planes. The BlackBerry created its own lexicon:
              ‘Crackberry’ – a BlackBerry addict; ‘BlackBerry Thumb’ – repetitive strain
              injuries caused by overuse of the tiny keyboard to send messages; ‘BlackBerry
              Eye’ – strain from trying to read the screen. Sherman had a new toy.

              sought me out occasionally for advice on where to invest. I explained my

                                     Bangs and whimpers
              It was the eve of battle. The matter looked likely to go to trial – the trial
              dates were set – the whole matter was set down for eight weeks. It was
              going to be an epic.
                  I was busy on a supplementary expert report. Stuart SC had managed to
              convince the judge that it was imperative in order to address the issues
              Sherman had raised. Complex technical arguments should be exchanged
              beforehand to speed up the trial; the judge had reluctantly agreed. ‘I insist
              that the Supplementary Report only address matters arising from the
              Claimant Expert’s Report. I don’t want new issues introduced at this late
              stage.’ He was still asking about the prospects of a settlement.
                  The supplementary report was our WMD – it was also my revenge.
              Sherman’s report had a number of glaring inconsistencies and errors. There
              were telling points in the supplementary, I thought. We would be able to
              establish that the transaction was incapable of fulfilling the function that the
              Indonesian noodle maker had wanted. Counsel had grasped the point
              immediately: ‘it was not of “merchantable” quality’; the best thing was that
              this was based on Sherman’s own analysis. I was still smarting from the sug-
              gestions of being a ‘purist’ and ‘theoretician’.
                  I worked diligently; I was scheduled to meet with the lawyers in London
              to finalize the report. Then, everything suddenly went quiet. Litigation
              always has quiet patches, but we were fast approaching the lodgement
              deadline for the Supplementary Report.

                  Eventually, I got hold of Morrison. ‘Been meaning to call you, old

              The matter would end with a whimper, the ‘bang’ of the trial would not
              occur. I was both relieved and shattered.
                  Over the next few days, I learned what had happened. There had been a
              change in management of the dealer, a series of trading losses and disputes
              with clients had emerged, a new CEO was concerned about ‘reputation
              risk’, fhe firm was going to be ‘clientcentric’. Neverfail was off ‘pursuing
              personal interests’.
                  Neverfail’s replacement – Porter – wanted to settle. The last thing he
              needed was an acrimonious court case with a client that the Financial
              Times and Wall Street Journal would cover in loving detail. It wouldn’t gel
              with the new client-focus mantra. He didn’t care about the money, he had
              taken substantial reserves against losses and potential damages claims. It was
              all Neverfail’s fault.
                  Killem & Billem put out the first tentative feelers. Morrison, sharp as
              ever, countered shrewdly – if the firm was serious then Porter himself
              should contact Morrison directly. Porter duly called. Morrison suggested a
              meeting between Porter and the chairman of the Indonesian noodle maker:
              it would be just the two of them – no advisors. Morrison was cagily trying
              to flush out the seriousness of the overtures.
                  The meeting took place. Porter flew to Jakarta especially for it. It went
              well, there was a meeting of minds. Porter explained that this was a case of
              a few ‘bad apples’, but that he needed to be paid a modest amount at least.
              This was to avoid the suggestion that the investment bank was admitting
              liability, which would excite several eager regulators. The two men shook
              hands on a deal.

              the relieved judge announcing the parties had come to a commercial settle-
              ment. The judge congratulated the parties and the ‘triumph of
              common-sense’. Both senior and junior counsel bemoaned the loss of a
              substantial amount of income.

                                   Knowns and Unknowns
              Derivatives are still hot: 25-plus years on they still continue to evolve. They
              are still causing controversy. New markets for hedging, making and losing
              money are emerging.
                  Derivatives linked to macro-economic indicators are being traded. Dealers
              trade exposure to gross domestic product, growth rates, rates of industrial
              production, retail sales, price indices and consumer confidence indices.
                  Macro-economic derivatives are based on a pari-mutuel auction system,
              the mechanism that underlies wagering on sporting events. Wagers are
              placed based on odds quoted, the person accepting the bets determines
              payouts if the wager predicts the outcomes correctly, there is no risk. The
              losing betters effectively pay the successful wagers plus the bookmaker’s
              profit, the odds quoted ensure this outcome. The bookmaker makes sure
              that the total premium received equals the subsequent payouts irrespective
              of the outcome of the event. Derivatives have gone full cycle. We really are
              off to the races.

                  Even the WFP (World Food Programme) had embraced derivatives.
              WFP was responsible for saving the starving. They proposed that they issue

              interest to the catastrophe bondholders. If there was low or no rainfall,
              then the WFP would be able to suspend interest payments or cancel princi-
              pal repayments on the bond. The saving in interest and principal would
              fund relief efforts.
                  I wasn’t sure how the catastrophe bonds would cover bad government
              or civil wars; traders thought a bad government or civil unrest index would
              be feasible. They were just trying to boost flagging volumes in the weather
              derivatives market. I wondered what the starving in the Horn of Africa
              would make of all this.
                  The people that I had worked with were mostly out of the business;
              they talked of the market changing. The ‘new’ world was ‘dull’, they
              bemoaned the lack of ‘characters’, there was no ‘innovation’. I didn’t agree
              with these sentiments: I believed that in reality little had changed. The old
              truths were still relevant. New generations of derivative traders were going
              to just discover them for themselves.
                  There were still the knowns and unknowns. There were many WMDs –
              new ones were invented every day. The lies – beautiful and true – were still
              the currency of trading. People still wanted to see the money, every day.
              The latest, greatest super models would still come up short in the crucible
              of markets. Perfect storms were lurking over the horizon: they would blow
              in suddenly, leaving death and destruction in their wake. Games without
              frontiers would still be played in the world of structured products. In equity
              markets, the pain would be shared and shared alike. The new credit markets
              were prospering, albeit under dubious premises. You had to give credit
              where credit is due. In the end, there were always the traders, the guns and
              the money. After all, this was the dazzling world of derivatives.
